frames.narration: Priya publishes a photo. Her app sends it to the feed API.
The API saves the post once and gets its id, p-501. As soon as it is stored, Priya's app is told the post is live. Nothing else has to finish first.
The API puts a small job on the queue: spread p-501 to Priya's followers. The queue holds it until a worker is free.

A worker takes the job, looks up Priya's 300 followers and adds the id p-501 to the top of each follower's feed list. Priya is below the popular-account threshold, so she is pushed. If the job ran twice, the ids would just be de-duplicated.
Later, Sam, who follows Priya and one celebrity, opens the app. His phone asks the feed API for his feed.
The API reads Sam's feed list, which already holds p-501, then pulls the newest posts of the celebrity he follows and merges both lists, removing duplicates. A ranking step orders the candidates.
The API fetches the details for the top 20 ids in one batch, mostly from the post cache. Likes and comment counts come from the same place, so they are current.
Sam sees a full page, including Priya's photo, with a cursor that marks the last post shown.
Sam scrolls down. His app sends the cursor back, and the API returns the posts after it. New posts arriving meanwhile cannot shift the page or repeat anything.
